Has the contract
been made for the present year?

Yes, the "Scotia," the same vessel as before, is making the trips.

Steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation in 1918 between the mainland and Magdalen Islands, $18,000.
Has the contract been signed, and is the vessel now on the route?

A boat is now on the route. The contract has been signed with Farquhar and Company, and the " Enterprise " is performing the service. She is the best, in fact the only boat, we could get. She is not as large as we would like, nor does she probably come up to the old standard of vessels that we had on this service. The contract, however, is in the hands of an excellent firm, and I think the service will be carried out as satisfactorily as it possibly can be under the circumstances.

Was there not an arrangement made with Captain Farquhar that the "Enterprise," being too small a craft for the service, would not be put on the route this year, but that a larger vessel would be built and put into commission?
We have not made any contract, or entered into any arrangement for the building of another vessel. Shipbuilding at the present time is a pretty expensive operation.
I understood from Captain Farquhar when he came here some weeks ago that he was ready to build a vessel if the department would give him a contract for a certain number of years.

I think that is true if we could have agreed upon the price of the vessel, and given a long contract, but we are not doing that in any of these services. We have to feel our way and do the best we can.
'Mr. MoTSAAC:	Is there, any steamer
plying where the " Enterprise " operated last year?

No. The only thing that has been done so far is that I have communicated with the "Enterprise," and the "Enterprise" will be able and willing to call at a number of these ports, and might possibly be able to give a very good service at these ports. I am in communication with the company in that respect.
Steam service between Mulgrave and Guys-boro, calling at intermediate (points, $5,500.

The service on this line has been performed for several years by the "Robert Cann," which was a very

good boat. She was withdrawn last year, and a much smaller boat was put on, the "Percy Cann." This boat is not suitable for the service; she is too small. I am not certain that the minister can find a better one at the present time. But it occurred to me that we will never be able to improve if we do not give notice prior to the expiration of the contract. Would it not he well if, three months before these yearly con-, tracts expire, tenders were asked for, so that owners of boats might have a chance to come in? The matter drifts along until the 30th March, or whatever date these contracts run out, and then the contract is renewed with the old company, and no one knows anything about it. The department might perhaps be able to improve the service here and there hy allowing others to tender, giving them ample time to do so, say three months prior to expiration of the existing contract. I ask the minister to consider that point.

In normal times I think that would be the proper course to pursue. In fact, we did pursue it before the war and asked for tenders. But during these times the route and the people on it may be thankful to get any sort of an old tub. There is not much chance for choice.
Steam service between Quebec and Gasp6 Basin, touching at intermediate ports, $8,500.
Would the minister explain the situation there?

The old boats,
as my hon. friend knows, passed off from the service last year in the latter part of the season, and although every effort was made to get a suitable boat for this service, in the end we had to take Hobson's choice. We did get a vessel which would undertake the service between Quebec and Gaspe Basin. The owner is Captain Tremblay, I think, and the boat is a fairly good boat, and will probably carry out the demands of the service.
Have you had an inspection made of the boat?

Yes, and she
is passed for the service.
Was a contract signed for that boat?
Between Quebec and Gaspe Basin?
Between, the Government and Captain Tremblay?
Yes.
I notice, Mr. Chairman, that you did not call item 175 for steam service between Quebec and Harrington and along the north shore.

We shall have
two boats on that service which will carry out the service on the schedule of last year, going down to the extremist point and giving the usual and customary service. We have been able to get a second boat on that line. It is rather a superior boat, a better one than I had expected to get.
Is that the "Elaine"?

The "Savoy"
and " Elaine " will perform the service along that coast. I am very glad to have got two such satisfactory boats as the department has been able to obtain.

But you have taken
the " Elaine " from the Gaspe route between Campbellton and Gaspd?
That is true.

Why did my hon. friend come to that decision? There is quite a traffic on the Baie deis Chaleurs. It is true that there is a railway on the coast, but the fishery business requires a boat in this section of the Bay, as there is a large traffic between New Brunswick and that part of Quebec. I understand that Mr. Evans, the proprietor of the Elaine, would have preferred to remain on the old route between Campbellton and Gaspe.

Several considerations come in there. In the first place, I was faced with the necessity of cutting down the total vote for steamship subventions and subsidies, and I have cut the vote down by nearly one half. The principles that I tried to base the deduction on were these: First, that the most important routes should be kept, and if it came up a question between a more important route and a less important, I should have to make the choice in favour of the most important one. The other principle was that where there was service by railway, the people would have to get along by railway service, and not indulge in the luxury of a double service. I realize there is some inconvenience in this arrangement; there are some ports which are a little distant from the railway, and which will be better served by having a vessel. But evidently we must come to a conclusion on the situation as it presents itself. The north shore service is not a paying service, as my hon. friend knows, but it is a necessary service. The people are there; they have no railways;
they are dependent on water communications, and whether there were 150,000 people down there or 5,000, we have to maintain a service; therefore, as between the service between Campbellton and Paspebiac. [DOT]and the service on the north shore, I had no hesitation, when I was able to sret the Elaine, in placing her on the more important service of the two. My hon. friend will find in the report on mail subsidies and steamship subventions a statement of the traffic carried between Campbellton and Gaspe. It has diminished so greatly that the payment of the subsidy demanded is not justified.
Because the boat was not of the same tonnage as in the old days.
I doubt that.

There is no question of luxuries in that section of the country; what the people want is opportunity to transport their fish. The railway runs along the coast but it does not touch all the little harbours and consequently it cannot always be depended upon. I protest against the cutting down of this subsidy and I hope that when better times come my hon. friend will revise his ideas and re-establish this line between Campbellton and Gaspe. My hon. friend knows 'that Baie dee Chaleurs is 'an attractive spot for tourists; there is no more beautiful section of the country in the whole of the eastern provinces. We must not discourage tourists from visiting that part of the country.

Nothing would delight me more than to see that route kept up; it is one of the scenic routes of our country. I myself have made the trip several times. But this is no time for tourists; in any case, tourists are not seeking that route at present. Moreover, you cannot get tourist trade unless you have a first-class vessel on the route. After the war is over, however, I hope that many things will come to pass.
The minister does not close the door completely, then?
Oh, no. I never close the door, even to my hon. friend.

I agree with what the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has said with reference to this matter. It is important that the steamer Elaine carry on the service between Campbellton and the northern part of the Gaspe coast. I have received a communication from a citizen of the town of Campbellton with reference to this subject, and submitted it to

the minister, who sent me the following reply, dated May 15:
The Steamer Elaine has gone upon the North Shore, St. Lawrence route, from Quebec eastward and is not available for the Campbellton-Gasp6 Service. The amount of freight- offering during the last two or three years on that route has been so small that it is not considered advisable to continue the expenditure. Though some inconvenience will no doubt be experienced, there is a railway which runs along that shore which will give a fair service' to most of the communities interested.
There is a great fishing traffic .along that coast, .and. the steamer Elaine could render the best .service. The cancelling of that steamer for the present summer would seriously affect the business in the northern part of New Brunswick and along the coast of Gaspe. We have not many .facilities for exporting fish along the Gaspe coast; many places are not touched by the railway. I hope that the minister will revise his ideas, not next year, but now, and give ue a service for the present summer.
Steam service between Rivifire du Loup, Tadoussac and other north chore ports, $6,000.

This is one. of
the services that I had to dispense with. The item seems to have got into the Estimates., however, and I movie that it Ibe struck out. The service referred to is between Riviere du loup, Tadoussac and other north shore ports. The vessels have deteriorated and changed hands. Last year we had no service because the vessels offering could not pass the examination necessary to entitle them to carry passengers. The whole amount of freight carried in one season on this route was only 142 tons. Had we retained the subsidy we could have bought all the freight, carried it on our backs to the different destinations, and still have had some money in pocket. I could no.t see that we should, in these .times, spend that money on a service which was of so
4 p.m. little real benefit. It is a convenience, but not a real necessity, .as the freight service shows.
Is the minister paying subsidies to the Canada Steamship lines?
No.	*

I was going to suggest
that he make arrangements with the Canada Steamship lines

the old Richelieu
Company-to have a vessel go to Rivifere du Loup once or twice a week
Why? You have the cars there.

You have in front of
Riviere du Loup the whole county of Char-

levois, the river Saiguenay, Cap-a-l'Aigle, Murray hay, and other important points. When the people of Riviere du Loup want to do business on the north shore they have to go the whole way around.

But the whole
of the freight carried there in a season was only 142 tons. You could carry it on a wheel barrow.
The trade has not had a chance to develop there.

This subsidy ha3 been, paid for at least ten years. The service has constantly depreciated; more than 1,000 tons was never carried on that route, and now the quantity is reduced to 142 tons. I would rather hire some man to carry that in a canoe, thus saving the public a good deal of money.

The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau) is not in his seat. He is interested in this service, because it is in his- riding. My hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) said that the Canada Steamships Lines' vessels should not call at Riviere du Loup, because there is no work for them to do. He is entirely mistaken as to that, because they are. calling there. Last year they called there at least twice a week. On. their way up to Chicoutimi they stopped every Saturday at Riviere du Loup, and on their way back they stopped there on every Sunday. This subsidy was rather for the encouragement of winter navigation on that part of the St. Lawrence river. The little boat that was being operated on that line was doing the service every month of the year, and the new experiment was a very successful one. I hope the minister will see bis way clear to restore this service in the near future in spite of what my hon. friend from Three Rivers says about it.
I would asik the minister to hold the matter open for a few minutes. I see the hon. member for Temis-oouata (Mr. Gauvreau) is now in. his seat.
Has the minister any good reasons for striking out this item?
I have just been endeavouring to state them.
Off the item is left in the estimates it will always be an inducement for some one to take steps to enter into a contract with the Government

I want to draw to my hon. friend's attention the flagellations which have been given to this and

former governments if they have put into their Estimates items which they do not purpose using. I am acting on the sense that has been drilled into me in part from the flagellations received from critic's on the other side of the House. Sudh criticism is quite fair. We cannot stuff our Estimates. There is not the least hope in the world of getting this service put on, ands, therefore, I do not want to carry the item in my Estimates. I shall, as my hen. friend suggests, keep an eye on the future, and if we can get a service which will justify a subsidy I shall be very glad to ask this House for an appropriation.

I shall take the drilling out of the minister by telling him that if the money is not spent, neither the Government nor any one else will he hurt, but if the item remains in the Estimates, it will be an intimation to some one that he should go to the minister and endeavour to enter into a contract. .

Seeing that the ministers are so hard worked already, why should my hon. friend want to keep this molasses point out to attract all those who would bother the minister in regard to some old tub or other? You cannot get anything but a tub these days.
Mr. IiEIMHEUX: Am I to understand the minister will restore this item to its proper place whenever a suitable boat is found for the route?
Sir GEORGE FOSTER, When sufficient grounds are given for the expenditure of money on this route, I shall be quite willing to ask the House for an appropriation.
Vote stricken from the Estimates.
Steam service from the opening to the closing of navigation In 1918, between Pictou, Mul-grave and Gheticamp, $7,500.
Has any change been made with respect to this route? I think it was the intention to drop Pictou.

The contract has not yet been signed and negotiations are still proceeding. My view was this-and I think it was approved-that the distance traversed between Pictou and Mulgrave was an unproductive part of the route, because, owing to the shallow water in the harbours along that coast, it was difficult for the boat to make uniform, stated calls. That being the case, a year or so ago, a small subsidiary vessel was given a subsidy to take over that part of the route, and I have put in the Supplementary Estimates an item for that service with the
view of dispensing with the coal-consuming part of the voyage for small freight between Pictou and Mulgrave and putting the strength of the larger vessel on the traffic which goes and comes between Mulgrave and the north. That traffic, at certain seasons of the year becomes congested even with the two boats whose services are given. The matter, however, has not been settled yet.

I am in receipt of several letters asking that this boat touch at Prince Edward Island. I quite agree with the minister that the call at Pictou is not desirable. I never could see any justification for it, because the boat could not, according to the minister's statement, call at any other ports along that route. If the boat would make one trip to one of the Prince Edward Island ports it would be of more service to the people, because we have more business with the island than with Pictou. We have already Mulgrave as a port of call. There is another matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention, and that is the demurrage at the port of Mulgrave. I have had some correspondence with the department with respect to that, and there are two things I would like the minister to bear in mind. First, there is no railway communication! with the northern ports. Secondly, navigation is only open for five months in the year. There is a very large population to be served north of Port Hood, and our difficulty is that in the fall of the year, from the first of September onwards, the steamer cannot make regular trips because there are no harbours on that coast. The steamer has sometimes to wait at Mulgrave two weeks in the stormy weather; watching for an opportunity to put out, and it is a very great hardship that our merchants should have to pay demurrage on the goods that are kept at Mulgrave until the boats can go out. During the last two years, and this session again, I have had some correspondence with the department and they have replied that concessions have been granted in this respect. I am quite satisfied that that is correct, but the minister will realize that a very large amount of money is paid in demurrage, particularly on account of flour, which comes in carload lots in the fall of the year and has to stay at Mulgrave for two weeks at a time. Of course, the consumer has to pay an increased price on that account, and I would ask the minister to look into this matter.
I shall be very glad to.

I understood the minister to say just now that he was making provision for the continued service of the small gasolene schooner between Pictou and Mulgrave, calling at ports in the county of Antigonish. I think the minister has received some correspondence requesting an increased subsidy. I have here figures showing the cost of operation during the past year and the amount of freight and subsidy received, which I will give the House so that the minister can refer to them on Hansard. The total 'amount received, including the subsidy for the operation oi this boat, last year was $2,878. The cost of gasolene and oil was $513.60, wages $960. victualling $320, insurance $100, repairs $423, other expenses, $60, deck and engine supplies, $74, depreciation, $90; making a total of $2,540.60, leaving a profit to the owner of $337.40. The boat is a good one, I am told, and worth perhaps $5,000 or $6,000, and the owner can hardly be expected to keep it in this service for the small profit he is making. The people along the coast fear that" the boat will be withdrawn if an additional subsidy is not given to the contractor. The boat performs a very important service in a local way, as many of these people are twenty miles from railway communication and they grow a good deal of farm produce, it being a farming district. They have been urged, of course, to increase their production during the war, and this boat is the only means they have of getting their produce to market. I have received letters from some of these people asking me to urge the Government to keep the boat in operation so that they can get their produce to market. I understand the contractor is 'asking for another $1,000. If that is too large a sum, the minister might consider adding half that amount to the subsidy in order to retain this boat in the service for the present year, I would again impress upon him the importance .of the service in a local way, because it would be a very serious matter for the people along that coast if the boat was withdrawn on account of the small sum that is being earned.	[DOT]

I have received a number of letters and telegrams from different people in St. John with reference to the steamer run by Connors Brothers, from St. John to Dipper harbour, Chance harbour, and Mace's bay. Only this morning I received a telegram from Manchester, Robertson & Allison, of St. John, protesting against the withdrawal of the subsidy for the steamer. Connors Brothers say that if

the subsidy is withdrawn they will take the steamer off 'the route. .This is a very important service, because the people in Dipper harbour, Chance harbour, Mace's bay and other small places along that shore depend entirely on this steamer for getting their goods from St. John. If the minister has already decided to withdraw the subsidy I would ask him to reconsider the matter. I am not aware how much the subsidy is, but it is important that this boat be kept on the route, both from the standpoint of Hie merchants of St. John and the people living in the places at which the steamer calls.

There is a very general idea that not much work is going on at the present time in the Interior Department, on account of there being no immigration, for one thing, and I think the minister should inform us whether it is not possible to reduce the numbers of employees and thereby curtail the expenses of his department. A few years ago an abnormal increase took place in the expenses of this department, under one of the minister's predecessors. Has the minister made any attempt to trim the Estimates this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am surprised that any one should have the impression that there was not much doing in the Interior Department. There is a way of cutting down the number of employees, and that way has been found and acted upon. The number of employees has been very considerably reduced.
The estimates, instead of going up, have been going down. There has been a very pronounced reduction. Nor has the work been going down at the same time; it is being carried on with as great efficiency and in volume almost as substantial as in previous years. The total reduction this year is some $454,000. There were eighty-one employees taken off. They were connected with the immigration service. The .Imimigration Department has been created, and consequently the volume of immigration does not affect the Department of the Interior work in any degree; formerly it affected it very heavily. The Interior Department has twenty-five branches, including that of Soldier Settlement. The soldier settlement work, which is now added to the work of the department, is by no means an unsubstantial or negligible

amount; it is a factor of great importance in the department, and so long .as it is needed it must continue to be a factor of importance. This item is the regular appropriation for 'Civil Government salaries. speechtext:
The New Welland Canal.
Now that the Country is committed to and constructing the New Welland Canal, it follows as a logical consequence tha/t the 2i5 (2>5-30) foot draft must ultimately be carried through to Montreal and tide water.
Pending this outcome the New Welland Canal appears as an unproductive load of $60,000,000 to ourselves, but of some benefit to our neighbours.
The St. Lawrence Canals-Deepening and Enlarging.
The St. Lawrence Canals are 14 foot draft. They begin at Cardinal and end at Montreal, embracing 45 miles of canals, including 18 locks. There are a-lso about 6>8 miles of river stretches.
The principle upon which the St. Lawrence canals depend for their depth and their further deepening is that of lowering the bed of the locks and canals, and also where necessary of the channels in the river stretches as well. The St. Lawrence canals being mainly along an International Waterway, the surface levels could not pe disturbed, I take it, without complications with vested interests and the United States.
Due to the foregoing conditions, I have estimated the cost of the deepening and the enlarging of the St. Lawrence canals and river stretches at about $150,000,000, as the construction work would be mainly under water work and much rock, of an expensive variety.
Deepening these canals necessarily entails "scrapping" existing works which have cost over $25,000,000, yet retaining their cost in the capitalization of the improvements.
im
As the opportunity is denied of# retaining depth on the St. Lawrence, by dams, the' alternative, the deepening and widening of the channels will accelerate the flow and cause earlier and longer low water.
Similar results have followed the continuous deepening of the St. Lawrence channel between Montreal and Quebec; the writer believes in barrages and locks to obtain depth there instead of continuing further deepening and also as a means of redeeming the evil results of the past methods.
Any tendency to lower Lake Ontario level would arouse United States protest and bring international complications; our own harbours on Lake Ontario would likewise be depreciated.
The Georgian Bay Canal.
The other alternative for a deep waterway from Port Arthur to Montreal has been the proposed Georgian Bay Canal.
The principle upon which the required depth in the Georgian Bay Canal is obtained is that of building dams and raising the level of the river, generally so providing the required depth not only in a channel but over a considerable width affording freer movement for vessels; a fairway.
The cost of the Georgian Bay Canal would now probably run to at least $150,000,000, due to the increased cost of living and of materials and the greater disturbance of established conditions.
The New Route.
I propose that the Great Lakes Route be accepted via the Welland to Cardinal at the head of the St. Lawrence rapids and canals.
I find that a deep canal can be, easily, carried through at Lake Ontario level from Cardinal to the vicinity of Ottawa, at which latter point it would require a 105 foot drop to the proposed level of the Ottawa river (say by three locks).
The canal on leaving the St. Lawrence would be through a 30 foot cut for three miles or so and then through level rich farming land as a level ditch following the contour of a gently sloping side hill.
The distance is about 50 miles from the St. Lawrence to the Ottawa, and would cost about $50,000,000. I am confident that the estimated cost would be much reduced on actual survey.
Using the Ottawa River-Ottawa to Montreal.
As already shown the attainment of the required levels in the Georgian Bay Canal, particularly in that portion of it which I propose to use, would be comparatively simple and inexpensive, due to its accomplishment mainly through the means of two dams and the consequent raising of the river levels.
' In proposing the adoption of that portion of the Georgian Bay Canal from Ottawa to Montreal, I would draw attention to the fact that there are only five locks which with the two dams afford long stretches of uninterrupted fairway.
Moreover the cost of the Georgian Bay Canal from Ottawa to Montreal as given in the Government estimates of that scheme is about $30,000y000, and owing to the work being all included in a few structures, the, margin of error in the estimates should not be very great. Europe, who go there to see the millions of birds- and there are literally millions of them. Some years ago some enterprising American and even. Canadian, 'business men started .to kill the- birds for use in ornamenting ladies' hats, and the eggs were stolen with a view to selling them. I do not know whether the Migratory Birds Act applies to those sea birds in the Gulf of St. Lawrence or not but I would ask my hon. friend to look into this matter and geit some information in regard to it. It would be a sorry day if these bird species were to disappear from Canada. When I say that there are millions of birds on this rock I do not exaggerate. The rock itself is about the size of the grounds around this building and there is enough space on the top of the rock, which is about three hundred feet^ high, to enable the lighthouse keeper to live there. He has a cow or two and he can have a few hens on the rock, but all the sides of the rock are inhabited by these birds. When the steamer goes nearby it is easy to see these birds by the millions, btrange to say, the first people to protest against the destruction of these birds were the Boston people. They are very good people as I know. I remember having read in some publication in, New England a protest against the destruction of these birds The Migratory Birds Act should apply to sea birds as well as to land ibirds. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
This is the first, vote
under the 'Soldier Settlement Act, 1917. The Soldier Settlement Board, appointed on January 31st last under the Act, consists of Mr. Samuel Maber, acting chairman, formerly head of the British Columbia Lands Branch of the Department
6 p'.m. of the Interior, who is serving on this board without extra -salary; Mr. C. F. Rowland, and Major Ashton. Mr. Maber is an old officer of the department and was appointed, in order that we might have the benefit of hi's wide experience and 'his excellent ability as a departmental officer. The activities of the board were first addressed to the taking care of such loans to returned soldiers as .would be necessary to enable them to do their spring seeding. Very satisfactory results have been accomplished. Applications have been disposed of to the number of 272. The advances in loans amount to $341,558, an average for each settler of $1,256. The Dominion land agencies throughout the country have been made agencies of the Soldier Settlement Board in order to avoid the expense of a duplicated organization.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
Have you adopted the
famous Van Home plan of radial colonies? Do you take the lands here and there with-

out regard to the number of returned soldiers applying for them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
We do not select the
land for them. The soldier .may settle on Dominion lands and get free entry. It is quite true that only a limited area of good land is available, but I t'h'ink there is enough to enable the board to be very useful to the soldier, for * time at all events. So far the board has not encouraged settlement in communities, the soldier may 'buy his own land anywhere, or if he has land and can give the board a first mortgage thereon, he is entitled to (a twenty-year loan at 5 per cent. This is 'the class of men who have so far chiefly availed themselves of the Act, although in some cases they have gone on unpat-*ented homestead lands. I cannot say how [DOT]many have made entries because our regulations have only recently been adopted. The machinery, however, is complete for taking care of entries made by returned soldiers.
Mr. PETER MeGIBBON (Muskoka): Is it the intention of the board to allot this land at present? If the area of available land is limited, what will be done in the case of soldiers who return two or three years hence?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: In governmental services we very seldom make arrangements for two or three years hence. It is sufficient to take care of the present and the immediate future. As a matter of general policy, however, it is my desire and the desire of the Government to work 'towards co-operative arrangements with the various provinces. Some progress has already been made to t^at end. We want to make arrangements whereby the assistance of the Dominion Government can be given to provincial plans and policies of soldier settlement, because we want to have regard to the fundamental principle of our constitution that the control of patented lands, civil rights and local administration is in the province.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: Is there any intention of giving the soldier in the province of Ontario assistance to locate on land or in such business as he might carry on?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
Yes. We have not yet got our organization in Ontario. We had first to take care of those districts from which the demands for land came, or where there was an immediate necessity of providing money, but we are now engaged in the work of establishing an organization in
Ontario. It will be available for all soldiers settling in Ontario who select, or who have, land in that province and can avail themselves of the privilege of the Act and give the Soldier Settlement Board a mortgage on their land. Amy one so settling can get a loan of $2,500 if the value of his land warrants that being done. As to any [DOT] scheme of soldier settlement generally, we hope, having in view the acquirement of land for the purpose, to work in co-operation with the Ontario Government.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: What basis of security is the Government taking for the loans they have made to the 272 settlers? I was in the office of the Soldier Settlement Board some time ago, and from the regulations as outlined to me by one of the commissioners, it did not seem to me that the proposal was of any great benefit to the soldier. I understood the purpose was to advance to the soldier settler about fifty per cent of the value of his land' or undertaking. He could borrow as much as that from any one, but he is, perhaps;, getting it at a little better rate of interest than be would be charged by a loan company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: He gets very consider-, able advantages. There is, of course, a limit to what can be done, because we must remember that the number of returned soldiers now is small as compared with what it will be, and that the standard of assistance set for one must be set for all. The soldier is entitled to get a loan, first of all on his soldier entry to which he does not get title. That loan nobody else can get. The soldier gets it at five per cent, repayable on the amortization plan in twenty years. He gets it without cost; he has no solicitor's fees to pay, as that is all taken care of by the board. And the soldier is able to get a larger per cent of the value of his property as a loan than would the ordinary settler.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: What per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: It varies, depending upon the quantity of lands immediately available for cultivation, on the revenue bearing power of the property more than on its immediate value in the market. But I think as high as 70 or 75 per cent has been advanced.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
The question asked by my hon. and gallant friend from Muskoka (Mr. Peter McGibbon) raises a question which I am not sure has sunk into the mind of either the minister or any other hon. member. My hon. friend has pointed

to the time "when the boys come home." At the present time there are vastly greater numbers overseas than there are in Canada, *and I am told there is a feeling overseas that the soldiers' interests should wait for consideration until the main body comes home. Here is a question again as to there being just so much available land, and it is very important that the Government should keep in mind that the main body is still overseas. As I understand the matter, soldiers are divided im feeling to some- extent. Two returned soldiers have called upon me lately protesting against claims that have been presented by selfconstituted champions of the returned soldiers.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: Who are they? Veterans?

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: These soldiers want the main considerations to wait until everybody is represented. I should like the House to keep this in mind when we are dealing with the returned soldier, that there is the quiet returned soldier and there is the one who meets with his fellows and passes resolutions which may be in his interest but with which the others do not agree. I do not know how far this difference extends, but it is there, and it is important for us to remember there are different kinds of returned soldiers and that they have different ideas as to what they want.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: I am at a loss to understand exactly what my hon. friend means by his language about the returned soldiers. Does he mean to say that some of them are so disreputable that we should not believe what they say? I understand there is a Great War Veterans' Association which speaks for the returned soldiers-generally. Does my hon. friend mean to say that the Government should not listen to the claims of the veterans, but should wait until the other soldiers who are still overseas return to Canada? What the hon. gentleman states is all mythical.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that when a soldier applies under this Act for a quarter-section he can take a homestead whether he has had one previously or not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: If he is entitled to a homestead, he gets one.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
I should like to know if any provision has been made so that a soldier can get a bonus of a few hundred dollars in lieu of applying for a homestead under this Act, and still have the right to [iMr. Mowat. ]
borrow $2,500. I have had a long experience in the West of men going on land under the tutelage of associations, or governments, or colonization companies, and as a rule, those people have failed. When an association has placed people on lands in the West and advanced money and taken mortgages on their farms in nine cases out of ten, or in nineteen cases out of twenty, those people have failed. I do not say that a man who is a farmer and who takes land under this Act will not make a success of it, but the great bulk of them will not be farmers. I don't care what conditions hedge around the grant of $2,500, or what precautions are taken to see that the men buy the right kind of horses and implements, in two or three years these men, who are forty or fifty miles away from a railway, will have spent that money and mortgaged their land, and the Government will have to take the land back and the money will be gone. The soldiers who take up land under this scheme will cost the country a lot of money in the end, for many of them will not make good, to put it mildly. I think it would be better for the country and more in the interest of the soldier in many cases, to give him the option of a cash bonus. T would ask the minister to consider that suggestion in the hope that when we meet next session something along that line will be done.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: This is the biggest question, I believe, that is before this country to-day, and I rather deprecate the idea of forcing it through like this. I think we should let the matter stand oiver until Monday to give hon. gentlemen an opportunity of expressing their views and hearing what the policy of the Government is in the matter.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: I would suggest that if we are not going to thresh it out now we had better rise and come back at eight o'clock, because we all want to get away on Wednesday, aftd if we devote Monday to discussing this matter that will be so much time lost for other legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to make a statement of policy in so far as it is possible at this date to do so, and to give all the details that can- be given. As to soldier settlement, there is only one statute now under which soldier settlement takes place. Provisions have been made with regard to a soldier taking an entry on Dominion lands, and on other lands, provisions have also been made for the administration of the Act, and the board is in

active operation. We have entered into negotiations, which I think are virtually completed, with one province, looking to an arrangement whereby that province assumes supervision of its soldier settlement and receives financial assistance from the Dominion to enable it to take care of by far the greater portion of the financial obligations thus entailed. We have now under review similar arrangements with other provinces, and I am in hopes that we shall succeed in coming to an agreement. I (believe that is the proper principle. I believe that toy local administration you will get the best results both for the soldier and for the country. I do not think any good is done by merely making an advance to the soldier and placing him on the land. I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Assiniboda (Mr. Turriff). I have seen too much of settlement tooth in Eastern and Western Canada,seen too many attempts to make men. farmers by capital advances', to have much faith in that method ever making a man a success on the land.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
Did the minister ever
conceive the idea of the Dominion Government cultivating the land for the first two years and letting the soldier learn how to farm during that time, and receiving his pay, so that at the end of the period he could take the land over with some knowledge of farming? There are other policies besides that of the minister that I would like to discuss.	.
Mr. (MEIGHEN:	That method has certainly been thought of 'by myself. It has been given more than thought by one province. The province of Ontario has adopted the principle of provincial assistance, accurately described, I think, toy my hon. friend. I make this suggestion to the committee: That having in mind the principle which animates my hon. friend from Park-dale (Mr. Mowat), having in mind the wisdom of not going too fast at the present time, having in mind the fact that the great majority of the soldiers are overseas, and that they should have a say in. the final disposition of this property as well as those at home, I think it would he well to watch the development of the project in Ontario, to see how it works out, and what lessons we can gain from it, before committing ourselves to any particular policy. The scheme in Ontario is well under way, and I think that before the next session of Parliament we can form very intelligent conclusions as to the success of the enterprise, and whether or not it embodies sound principles of settlement. Fot the present I think it would he well to keep in mind the main goal of making the soldier settlement a success by personal supervision on the part of the board both as regards unpatented land and land owned by the soldier, and confine outside operations .to an endeavour to make suitable arrangements with the provinces whereby they can carry on successful provincial schemes.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
Would an 'arrangement
with other provinces similar to that made with Ontario involve giving to the provinces their natural resources?

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.

Ontario has a policy of its own along the line stated by my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy), of taking an area of land, purchased or its own property, improving that area, and making individual settlements out of it by the utilization of soldier labour, paying the soldiers for their work with a view to selling them the land ultimately on terms.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: Will it be optional for the soldier to come under a provincial or a Dominion scheme? Has he to take up land in a particular province? The Dominion lands are in Western Canada.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: As we are dealing with the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs, I wish to refer to- a matter about which I spoke to the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). It is in connection with certain charges against Mr. Taylor, now agent at the Crooked Lake Indian Deserve. Under the old1 system I had the patronage of the Government for seven years and I never in my life asked for the dismissal of' a single individual, and never have I countenanced anything in that way. But I must admit that on the present occasion I feel that it is time that an official of the department who has not been dismissed should1 be dismissed, and I trust that the department will take some action in the matter. Last fall and winter I heard so many complaints about this agent, Mr. Taylor, that I thought it would be well to go into the case.

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext: Where is he located?

subtopic: MEMORANDUM RE AN 'ECONOMIC ROUTE FOR COMPLETION OF INLAND DEEP WATERWAY.
speechtext:
A short distance north of Broadview near where I live. I therefore invited some of the people who were complaining of his actions to meet me at Broadview on a certain occasion. I asked Mr. Boyer also, the clerk of the agency, who was more or less conversant with what had 'been going on, to meet me there. I did not make any attempt to have a thorough investigation into the affairs in connection with the agency, but while I was satisfied that I had only touched the fringe of the wrong-doing of the agent I felt that I had heard enough to justify me in asking the department to immediately suspend the agent pending inquiry, to institute a thorough inquiry into his conduct, and also to recommend that the investigation be not placed wholly in the hands of Commissioner Graham. I did not wish then, nor do I wish now, to- question the fact that Mr. Graham is a very competent official, but there were what appeared to me good reasons why Mr. Graham should

not be the sole investigator in that particular case. The department provided for an investigation by Mr. Graham alone, but did not suspend the agent, thereby leaving the people from whom the evidence against him must mainly come under the thumb of the accused'. That was not a correct principle. This investigation was, to my mind, anything but thorough. I believe, however, that the evidence brought out not only justified the dismissal of the official but made it the duty of the department to dismiss him. The Indian Act, section 42, provides among other things that:
No official or employee connected with the Inside or Outside Service of the Department of Indian Affairs .... shall without special license in writing of the Superintendent General trade with any Indian or sell to him directly or indirectly any goods or supplies, Cattle or other animals.
Section 131 provides that in case of violation- of the provisions of this section, the person so violating shall be liable to a fine equal in- -amount to double th-e -sum received for -the goods, supplies, cattle or other -an-imaiis sold.
And, in addition to that, the costs of the prosecution.
Mr. Taylor -admits purchasing the following goods from Indians:	-
1.	Hide from Old Francis.
2.	Hide from Kenowekesequake.
3.	Pony from Stevenson.
He -admits having made the following Sales to Indians:
1.	Horse to Stevenson, bought at $142, sold to Indian at $175.
2.	Horse to Kenoweswanwetang, which he claims belonged to his father's estate.
3.	Horse to Zac Le Rat. Mr. Sugden says Mr. Taylor (bought (this horse from him at $126. This is not denied by Taylor. The clerk says the hooks show the horse was sold at $160. This price is not denied -by Mr. Taylor.
4.	Horse sold to Angus Alex. Mr. Sugden says he sold this horse to Taylor for $120, and the clerk says the books show the horse was sold at $140. Mr. Taylor does not deny either of these prices.
5.	Horse to Tom Shesheep. Mr. Taylor says this horse belonged to his father's estate.
6.	Horse to Harry Faval. Mr. Taylor says this was one of his father's horses.
Here are nine, or if we count the two deals with 'Stevenson as one trade, at least eight, distinct violations of a very important provision of the Indian Act. It seems to me that the policy of maintaining -an Indian Agent in charge of a reserve who habitually violates one of the most important provisions of the Act is one that cannot be countenanced by any one who wants to see the Department of Indian

Affairs carried on as it .should/ be. Mr. Taylor said:
I knew that the regulations prohibited me from dealing with Indians.
He showed nothing but contempt for the law and the department, /shows little more respect for it in continuing in office an agent who thus openly and repeatedly violated one of the most important provisions of the Act under which he is working. Harry Cameron, the interpreter, who can hardly be accused of unfriendliness to the agent, in answer to a question says:
The agent often makes deals with the Indians, and I don't think he loses anything. I don't know how much he makes.
Neither do I know how much he makes nor is the department likely to know how much he makes until a more thorough investigation is held. The investigation, however, shows that in three of the deals referred to he sold for $475 horses that he had bought for $388, and so far as I can find the department has not punished him, or even asked for a refund of the difference.
Notwithstanding these many serious violations of the provisions of the Act, Mr. Graham in his report glosses them over by saying:
The Department's regulations state that no employee shall trade with the Indians, but I don't think that this regulation was intended to apply to employees purchasing berries, baskets, wood, water or hay for their own private stock on the reserve, and if not I cannot see that purchasing a hide to be used as a robe for one's family should be considered as exceptional.
Evidently Mr. Graham seems to think it is	only	in	exceptional	cases	that lawbreakers should be punished. I think it is	only	in	exceptional	oases	that they
should be allowed to go scot free. Further on he says with regard to those breaches of law:	_
There is no doubt at all but Mr. Taylor has been exceedingly indiscreet in his dealings with the Indians. He should have obtained permission from you before selling horses to them.
" Indiscreet " 'is a very gentle term to use in this connection. Still I suppose every law-breaker is " indiscreet." Speaking of Taylor's deal with Stevenson, Mr. Graham says:
I am satisfied there was no intention on his part to make anything out of the Indian.
This in face of the fact that Taylor himself says:
I consider I made $27.30 assuming the pony was worth $50.

f

And he does not appear from the evidence to question the fact that the pony he got from Stevenson in the trade was worth $50.
Mr. Graham, during the investigation, made this statement:
The late farm instructor Sugden states you have been in the habit frequently of using the Government blacksmith shop (at the agency) for repairing your own farm things, using coal and iron, the property of the department. Tour own men and yourself did the work.
Mr. Taylor says in reply:
I do not remember working there myself, but my man used it two or three times doing private work.
No denial is made of the charge of applying the Government coal and iron to his own use. Mr. Sugden, in his statement, says that Mr. Taylor had his private threshing engine repaired in. that way, .but no notice of this was taken at the investigation. With regard to the tools said to have been taken from the Government threshing outfit, and afterwards found in Mr. Taylor's possession, that gentleman said, in answer to a question.:
Yes, I had the tools, they are still in my car in the shed, I think.
Regarding the charges of using the Government blacksmith shop, the Government coal, and Government iron and tools, Mr. Graham says in his report:
Mr. Taylor admits his hired man used the Government blacksmith shop on two or three occasions doing private work. He also admits having used on his own motor, tools that belonged to the threshing outfit. It seems to me this latter charge is ridiculous.
It will be noticed that Taylor says, with regard to the tools: " I have the .tools," while /Mr. Graham softens it down by saying he had used them. The charge may, in Mr. Graham's mind, be ridiculous, but I am satisfied that had any one else appropriated the Government's property in this way, and had the fact come to Mr. Graham's attention, the offender would have been prosecuted for theft. I think these repeated breaches of the provisions of the Indian Act, and improper dealings with Government property should have insured the dismissal of the agent. I would not be taking up the time of the House, however, but for the fact that s/erious charges of immorality are made against this agent. I am satisfied that even the faint-hearted investigation held disclosed a state of affairs that called for his dismissal. It seems to me the House will agree that this is a very serious thing on,



the part of an Indian agent. We know that the Indians are somewhat susceptible people, and it seems to me that it ought to be understood at all times that no one should be employed in the capacity of agent against whose moral conduct anything can be said. I am told that these charges of immorality against Indian agents and officials are very common-in fact, I am given to understand they are levelled against all of them. That may or may not be true, but as far as regards the particular locality of which I speak-and I have been living there for the last thirty-five or forty years- this is the first time I ever heard any suggestion of the kind with respect to the Indian agents on the Crooked Lake or Assiniboine reserves.
M'r. Graham appears to recognize the incompleteness of the evidence forthcoming, but seeks to lay the blame on some one else. So far as I know I was the only person laying any charges, but Mr. Graham chooses to ignore me altogether, and the investigation was over before I knew it was being held. Mr. Graham tries to throw the responsibility for what happened on Mr. Boyer, the clerk, and says of him:
He Iras had every opportunity to have witnesses at the investigation to corroborate the charges made by the Indians and others, but there were none, and it was only a case ot one person's word against another's.
Now Mr. Boyer has advised me that on the day the investigation commenced, Mr. Graham and his secretary arrived at the agency about 2 p.m., and they said nothing whatever to Boyer about any impending investigation until about 5.30 p.m., when that gentleman wa:s preparing to go to his home. Then it was that he received the first intimation that an investigation was to be held. He was instructed by Mr. Graham to be present at the office at 7 p.m., when the investigation was commenced. Boyer has assured me that it was never intimated to him that he was to be in any way responsible for the prosecution, or that he had any authority to call witnesses. Mr. Boyer appears to have had connection with only five charges.. On three of these Mr. Graham finds the charges proved. On another, with regard to oats, he finds Mr. Taylor's actions irregular and unbusinesslike.
I dislike very much taking up the time of the House with regard to any matter of this kind. I dislike to find fault with any official of the Government, hut I believe the situation is so serious there that the dismissal of this official is necessary. I do not propose to stand by while any offi-
IMr. Thomson.]
cial, in a locality so near to my home as this is, acts in the manner in which this official has acted, without raising my protest against it.

speechtext: The agent who occupied this position some years ago is still at Heatherton. He was dismissed after the change of Government in 1911 in order to make room for the friends of the late administration. He had been a satisfactory officer. As this is not a partisan Government I tho lgbt that pe.haps the six or seven years he has been out of office would be sufficient punishment tor having voted Liberal, and that the minister might consider the question of reappointing him. I do not know whether it is in order to say anything, because now theie is no patronage and I am not at liberty to write a letter to say that he is a good man. He held office for a number of years with great satisfaction to everybody and he was removed in 1911 with a host of others in .Nova Scotia. I think he would take the office back if it were offered him.
